item.title: TSX extends weekly decline as financials, consumer-related shares fall
item.description: Canada’s main stock index added to its weekly decline on Friday as losses for financials and consumer-related stocks offset gains for energy, with recent turbulence globally in AI-linked stocks keeping risk appetite in check.
item.dc:creator: Fergal Smith
item.content:encoded: Canada’s main stock index added to its weekly decline on Friday as losses for financials and consumer-related stocks offset gains for energy, with recent turbulence globally in AI-linked stocks keeping risk appetite in check. The S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) ended down 185.27 points, or 0.5%, at 35,788.18, its lowest closing level since October 14. For the week, the index was down 1.1%. "It's been a risk-off week," said Greg Taylor, chief investment officer at PenderFund Capital Management. "The TSX has held in better than some other indices for the last little bit," Taylor said. "It's probably been held up by the energy sector but we're starting to see some weakness in banks and some other parts of the market this week." Heavily weighted financials (.SPTTFS) fell 0.9% on Friday, with shares of Manulife Financial Corporation (MFC.TO) down 2.9%. Food and pharmacy retailer Loblaws Companies (L.TO) lost 2.8%, contributing to a 2.2% decline for consumer staples. The materials sector (.GSPTTMT) , which includes metal mining shares, fell 1.2% as gold hit a three-month low ahead of a Federal Reserve interest rate decision next week. The [USN:L6N46911N TEXT:"Bank of Canada"] is also due to make an interest rate decision next week. The majority of economists polled by Reuters expect the central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% and follow with one more hike by the end of March. Telecom operator [USN:L8N4691GI TEXT:"Rogers Communications"] reported third-quarter profit above estimates. Still, its shares were down 2.3%. Energy was the only one of 10 major sectors to end higher, adding 2.1%. [USN:L6N469125 TEXT:"US crude oil futures"] settled 3.8% higher at $103.27 a barrel after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East. US President Donald Trump signed an order to [USN:L6N46914T TEXT:"remove 50% tariffs"] on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products.

item.title: Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears
item.description: With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel.
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Renshaw, Leah Douglas
item.content:encoded: With the November midterm elections fast approaching, President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel. His administration has offered billions of dollars to farmers, relaxed rules for truckers, [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"eased sanctions"] on Russian fuel and pressured European allies to release emergency stocks. Yet diesel prices rose again last week, leaving Trump spending political and financial capital without delivering the relief his party wants as voters go to the polls. Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress, and high costs are a major concern for voters. Nearly 80% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame"] Trump for higher costs, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. US diesel prices [USN:L6N45Z19G TEXT:"rose nearly 10 cents a gallon"] in the latest week to an average of $6.28, reversing two weeks of declines and remaining near record highs, according to the Energy Information Administration. Diesel in the last two months has become a central issue not only in the midterms but as a catalyst driving up already-elevated US inflation. The fuel is critical for farmers, construction companies, freight operators and more, and government data last week showed its rise was partly behind hefty increases in delivery costs, early-stage food production costs and [USN:L6N461198 TEXT:"even toy prices"]. The political pressure is particularly acute in traditionally Republican Farm Belt states like [USN:L6N44F10S TEXT:"Iowa"] and [USN:L6N45F193 TEXT:"Kansas"], where rising fuel and fertilizer costs, trade disruptions and weak farm economics have fueled discontent among some of Trump's core supporters. Trump has promoted his diesel measures at campaign [USN:L1N45Q06H TEXT:"rallies"] across the region. He signed an executive order onstage in Nebraska allowing red-dyed diesel to be used in highway vehicles and announced $8 billion in new farm aid during a rally in Kansas on Monday. The measures illustrate the trade-offs Trump is accepting in pursuit of near-term relief. The new aid adds fresh strain on federal spending, while the Russian fuel move risks helping Moscow finance its war in Ukraine. Pressure on European allies to release emergency stocks, backed by a threat to restrict US diesel exports, has created diplomatic friction. “The president tends to discount long-term losses over short-term gain, and I am skeptical if there is any short gain to be had here,” said Chris Borick, a pollster and political scientist at Muhlenberg College in Pennsylvania. The White House attributed high diesel prices to “pre-existing issues,” including years of refinery closures and damage from Russia's war in Ukraine, while defending Trump's efforts to ease costs. “The President wants diesel prices to fall, which is why he has taken historic actions to save American farmers, truckers, and workers every hard-earned penny," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said. SKEPTICISM AND UNANSWERED QUESTIONS One of Trump's most direct attempts to lower diesel costs has struggled to gain traction. Trump signed an executive order this month [USN:L1N461138 TEXT:"allowing truckers to use red-dyed diesel"], typically intended for off-road use such as farm equipment, for highway driving while temporarily avoiding certain federal tax reporting and record-keeping requirements. But the IRS has not eliminated the federal diesel tax, instead temporarily waiving related reporting requirements and penalties through year-end, leaving uncertainty for truck stops and fuel sellers. David Fialkov, top lobbyist at NATSO, a trade group representing the largest US truck stop operators, said members appreciate Trump's effort to tackle diesel costs but that the guidance remains "murky" and carries too much risk. "I really don’t see any of these dyed diesel announcements making a meaningful dent in diesel prices," Fialkov said. Trump is also turning to federal payments to cushion some of the constituencies feeling the pain. Government payments to farmers were already expected to top $47 billion this year, buoyed by commodity payments and $12 billion in tariff relief [USN:S0N3VI02L TEXT:"distributed "]by the US Department of Agriculture earlier this year. The $8 billion farm relief program would push the total to a record $55.4 billion, exceeding the previous high of $45 billion in 2020, when farmers received pandemic assistance. The payments can help farmers manage higher costs and lost sales but do not directly address the market disruptions driving up fuel and fertilizer prices. They also raise questions about taxpayer spending to compensate producers for damage that farm groups say is linked partly to the administration’s own trade and foreign policies. “This is the second round of emergency aid this year to address losses that were largely foreseeable,” National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said. “Trade disruptions and rising fuel costs tied to conflict abroad have put family farmers in a difficult position, and one-time payments can't provide the stability they need to plan for the future.” The aid will arrive after the November 3 election, and likely not reach farmers until the end of the year, USDA official Richard Fordyce [USN:L6N4690W3 TEXT:"told Reuters"] on Friday. FRICTION OVER RUSSIAN FUEL Some of Trump's efforts to increase diesel supplies carry geopolitical trade-offs. His decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel that were designed to restrict Moscow’s energy revenues and limit its ability to finance its war in Ukraine has [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"drawn bipartisan criticism"] -- and raised questions about whether the move will meaningfully lower US fuel prices. Trump has defended the sanctions relief as necessary to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and to release American prisoner Stephen Hubbard. As the administration's intervention efforts have failed to lower fuel costs, Trump has sought to shift blame toward Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskiy rather than the Iran war ahead of the elections. Analysts say the Iran conflict has been the much bigger driver of the diesel price spike, disrupting global oil flows and refined-fuel supplies, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have helped tighten supplies but played a more limited role in the price. “I sort of see it as a blame-shifting kind of scapegoating operation, more than a genuine attempt to moderate prices in the lead-up to the election,” said Edward Fishman, director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center at the Council on Foreign Relations.

item.title: Macron says Paris suburb shooting that killed one person was terrorist and racist act
item.description: A gunman killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in a shooting in a Paris suburb that French President Emmanuel Macron described as a "terrorist and racist" attack.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: A gunman killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in a shooting in a Paris suburb that French President Emmanuel Macron described as a "terrorist and racist" attack. "What happened today is, I am telling you, a turning point, because it is the first time we have had a terrorist act that was planned to kill our compatriots, our children, based on the colour of their skin or their religion," Macron told reporters. The shooting happened earlier on Friday when the gunman fired an automatic weapon at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children's playground in Trappes, on the Paris outskirts. Officials said a 39-year-old suspect, whom they named as Kevin T, had been arrested. His family surname was not given, as is common practice in such criminal inquiries in France. The shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France, after nationwide protests [USN:L1N46908B TEXT:"turned violent"] last Saturday and before further demonstrations this coming weekend. Some far-right politicians have blamed immigration for looting and vandalism in a number of French cities on October 17. Macron said the gunman had deliberately chosen not to fire upon some people due to their skin colour and appearance. The anti-terrorism prosecutor's office, known as PNAT, formally opened an investigation into the shooting. PNAT can [USN:L8N3SB03W TEXT:"take over any criminal investigation"] it believes meets the criteria for terrorism, including violence inspired by far-right ideas. Terrorism sentences are tougher, and counter-terrorism forces have greater investigative powers. Broadcaster BFM said the wounded girl had been hit eight times and was in serious condition. Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh, whose parents came from Morocco, said the shooting was "racist" and "Islamophobic." "The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law," said Rabeh. Rabeh called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that "ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts." Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of nearby La Verriere, said the suspect was "of a European type." Rabeh said two of the victims were of African and North African origin, respectively, and did not provide details about the backgrounds of the other victims. Video images showed the suspect's car riddled with bullets.

item.title: UK watchdog restricts six private credit firms over anti-money laundering controls
item.description: Britain's financial watchdog said on Friday it had imposed restrictions on six private credit lenders over concerns about their anti-money laundering controls, limiting their ability to take on new customers and enter into new lending arrangements.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Britain's financial watchdog said on Friday it had imposed restrictions on six private credit lenders over concerns about their anti-money laundering controls, limiting their ability to take on new customers and enter into new lending arrangements. The restrictions curb the ability of the firms, which are relatively small, to take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements and, in some cases, accept payments from existing customers, the Financial Conduct Authority said. The FCA has promised to increase scrutiny of unregulated lenders - called Annex 1 firms - in the wake of the [USN:S8N3ZD0BP TEXT:"collapse "]earlier this year of UK-based property lender Mortgage Financial Solutions.

item.title: Gold set for steep weekly loss as rising oil prices bolster Fed rate hike bets
item.description: Gold fell to a three-month low on Friday and was headed for its steepest weekly decline in over four months as higher energy prices fueled inflation concerns and reinforced US rate hike expectations ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting.
item.dc:creator: Noel John, Anushree Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: Gold fell to a three-month low on Friday and was headed for its steepest weekly decline in over four months as higher energy prices fueled inflation concerns and reinforced US rate hike expectations ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting. Spot gold fell 0.6% to $3,998.35 an ounce by 11:20 a.m. EDT (1520 GMT), slipping below the $4,000 mark for the first time since mid-July and touching a session low of $3,975.23. Bullion has fallen 4% this week, putting it on track for its worst week since June. US gold futures for December delivery settled 1.3% lower at $4,007.90 per ounce. Brent crude touched a more than five-month high, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies. "Heightened inflation concerns suggest that major central banks of the world won't be able to ease monetary policies as quickly as they want to. All that's working against the gold and silver market bulls at present," said Jim Wyckoff, a market analyst at American Gold Exchange. The selloff in technology stocks has also led to margin calls for equity traders and investors, prompting them to sell gold and silver assets, Wyckoff said. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq touched their lowest in five weeks on Friday as caution prevailed after a sharp selloff in AI-linked stocks. Meanwhile, traders largely expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, although stronger-than-expected US [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"consumer"] and [USN:L1N4610KT TEXT:"producer"] inflation data released last week bolstered the case for tighter monetary policy later this year. They see a 92% chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged next week and a 78% probability of a December hike, according to CME's FedWatch Tool. FEDWATCH The US Personal Consumption Expenditures report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, on October 29 could offer further insight. Elsewhere, gold buying picked up in India this week as lower prices during the major Dussehra festival boosted purchases and lifted premiums, while physical demand in top consumer China was steady even as cautious consumers continued to curb jewellery spending. [GOL/AS] Among other metals, spot silver slid 1% to $53.97 per ounce, and palladium dropped 0.5% to $1,048.31, hitting their lowest since November 2025 and June 2025 respectively. Spot platinum fell 0.9% to $1,555.84 per ounce, its lowest since July. All three metals were headed for weekly declines.

item.title: Euro sinks on French debt worries, yen gains for week on AI rout
item.description: The euro fell on Friday and was on track for a weekly loss against both the US dollar and the yen as a selloff in French government bonds pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011.
item.dc:creator: Karen Brettell
item.content:encoded: The euro fell on Friday and was on track for a weekly loss against both the US dollar and the yen as a selloff in French government bonds pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone [USN:L6N4680QK TEXT:"sovereign debt crisis"] in 2011. The Japanese yen was headed for a weekly increase against the greenback as it benefited from safe-haven flows from the selloff in AI stocks on Thursday. The dollar index was little changed on the week. The euro was hit by concerns about growing unrest in France and the country's worsening budget problems. France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests [USN:L1N4690GR TEXT:"on Saturday"], Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. The country also faces the threat of a [USN:L8N4682H3 TEXT:"rating downgrade"] by Moody’s on Friday. "The pressure in the European bond market has eased today, but Moody’s review of France’s debt rating late today poses a challenge, and although the Macron government has threatened military assistance to quell the social unrest, more activity is likely this weekend," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Global Forex. The euro was last down 0.21% at $1.1191 , set to end the week 0.43% lower. It fell more sharply against the yen, touching its lowest level since October 2025 at 175.08 yen . It was last down 0.11% against the Japanese currency and on track for a weekly decline of 1.1%. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.25% to 101.82 and was headed for a weekly gain of 0.03%. The yen weakened 0.1% to 156.9 per dollar and was on track for a weekly gain of around 0.7%, its best week since mid-September. "The yen has continued to trade at stronger levels at the end of this week, encouraged by more risk-off trading conditions," said Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG. CENTRAL BANK POLICY MEETINGS IN FOCUS Traders are looking to next week's policy meetings at the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan. All three are expected to leave rates unchanged, but investors will look for clues on the future path of policy. Fed funds futures traders trimmed bets on a December hike after Thursday's stock market selloff, though they still see an 81% chance of such a move, according to LSEG data. Traders see a 66% chance of an ECB hike in December. Investors will scrutinize any hint of the [USN:L8N4651KP TEXT:"rate outlook"] after ECB President Christine Lagarde said in late September that a moderate policy response to inflation was appropriate. Purchasing Managers' Index data showed private-sector growth in the euro zone slowed in October to its [USN:L6N4690J4 TEXT:"weakest pace"] in four months, hurt by a renewed contraction in France. "The drop brings the PMIs back in line with other growth indicators, in our view, rather than suggesting downside risks from here," Giada Giani, an economist at Citi, said. "France remains a drag, but the rest of the euro area remains resilient." In Japan, data on Friday showed annual core consumer inflation [USN:L4N46724Q TEXT:"exceeded"] the central bank's 2% target in September for the first time in nine months. The reading points to broadening price pressures and strengthens the case for a near-term rate hike, analysts said. Traders are pricing in 61% odds of a BOJ hike in December.

item.title: Stocks mixed, day after AI-related selloff; oil prices rise again
item.description: Stock indexes were mixed on Friday, with tech shares edging higher after the previous day's selloff, while Brent crude oil rose to its highest in more than five months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Valetkevitch, Marc Jones
item.content:encoded: Stock indexes were mixed on Friday, with tech shares edging higher after the previous day's selloff, while Brent crude oil rose to its highest in more than five months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. The Nasdaq was up 0.2% after starting the day lower, while the Dow was last down about 1%. An index of semiconductors (.SOX) was up about 1%. It posted its biggest daily percentage drop since June on Thursday after a report from Meta Platforms (META.O) reignited worries about the AI trade. It's been "a very volatile week," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth in Boston. "After Meta's report, there's still anxiety over the AI trade to a certain extent," he said. "But also, we continue to be in a place where things look like they're getting worse, not better, in the Middle East. That moves energy prices higher, which is obviously going to end up being a significant headwind for economic activity." Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia [USN:L1N46903W TEXT:"fanned fears"] over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where United Arab Emirates authorities also reported an oil spill. US crude rose 2.56% to $102.02 a barrel and Brent climbed to $116.27 per barrel, up 2.74%. European natural gas prices jumped. AMEX, TELECOM SHARES FALL Investors were digesting corporate earnings news. American Express (AXP.N) shares fell 3.5% after it [USN:L4N4690WS TEXT:"reported"] results and its CEO said the company had good momentum, but needed to become a more "agile and efficient" organization. Telecom company shares, including Verizon (VZ.N) , dropped after a Bloomberg News [USN:L4N4682CX TEXT:"report"] that SpaceX (SPCX.O) was in talks with cellular infrastructure companies about launching a US wireless carrier program. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 476.25 points, or 0.9%, to 52,391.73, the S&P 500 (.SPX) eased 11.14 points, or 0.14%, to 7,652.96 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) rose 52.51 points, or 0.21%, to 26,062.75. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) fell 1.64 points, or 0.15%, to 1,121.29. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index fell 0.4%. Asia's bourses steadied overnight, with South Korea's KOSPI (.KS11) ending its session higher after shedding as much as 4% earlier. US Treasury yields rose a day after the benchmark 10-year yield registered its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years, but remained under 5%. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was last up 3.7 basis points at 4.992%. The 10-year yield is down about 11 basis points on the week and on pace for a third straight week of declines, its longest run lower since June. EURO FALLS The euro fell and was on track for a weekly loss against both the US dollar and the yen, while euro zone bonds stabilized after recent volatility. Investors' focus has been on concerns over France's finances. French yields , which were down 5 basis points at 5.04%, have risen nearly 27 bps this week, the most of any major euro zone country and the most in a week since late May. A selloff in French government bonds this week pushed the country's debt risk premium to its highest level since the euro zone sovereign debt crisis in 2011. France [USN:L1N4690GR TEXT:"will deploy"] 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. The country faces the threat of a rating downgrade by Moody’s later on Friday. The euro was last down 0.12% at $1.12 , set to end the week 0.35% lower.

item.title: Oil prices jump $3 on Houthi attacks, oil spill, highest settlement since April
item.description: Oil prices settled more than $3 higher on Friday, their highest in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Jao
item.content:encoded: Oil prices settled more than $3 higher on Friday, their highest in nearly six months after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East, where UAE authorities also reported an oil spill. Brent crude futures settled at $116.72 a barrel, up $3.55 or 3.14%, their highest since April 29. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $103.27 a barrel, up $3.80 or 3.8%. Brent finished the week up 6% and WTI ended 2.3% higher. "Fears of supply disruptions drove the advance after Iranian-backed Houthi rebels carried out a series of attacks across Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure," said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial. On Thursday, Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) [USN:L1N46809Q TEXT:"ordered the evacuation"] of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported. Fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis. An oil spill from a tanker [USN:L1N469029 TEXT:"was detected"] off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said. It did not say what caused the spill and authorities have not identified the tanker involved. ATTACKS ON VESSELS Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No. 2 supertanker was [USN:L1N45V0GU TEXT:"struck"] by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles (24 km) west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. "The market is concerned about these continued Iranian attacks on tankers that we've seen increase over the last week," said Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "While there has been an increase in oil transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz, that could change at any minute." Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. October has been the [USN:L8N4682UH TEXT:"worst month for attacks on commercial shipping"] in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US could [USN:L6N469109 TEXT:"end the war with Iran quickly"], but said perhaps Washington should allow the conflict to gradually wind down. STRATEGIC RESERVE RELEASES The US Department of Energy said it had [USN:L1N4690OW TEXT:"authorized"] an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption affecting Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana. The SPR is already at the lowest level since 1982 after President Donald Trump tapped it as the US war on Iran disrupted supply lines. Trump's predecessor, President Joe Biden, also tapped the SPR following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Elsewhere, Germany's national oil stockpiling agency EBV circulated a tender [USN:L6N469129 TEXT:"to sell"] diesel, heating oil and crude oil volumes from strategic reserves. This marks Germany's first oil releases from strategic reserves since G7 countries, under pressure from Trump, agreed to do so at the start of October. On Thursday, the head of Libya's National Oil Corp told Reuters that an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port had been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields. Ship tracking data showed the first Russian diesel [USN:L1N4690EB TEXT:"bound for the US"] since Moscow and Washington reached an export agreement was aboard a tanker heading for New York. Trump announced the [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"deal"] this month as part of efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3. US energy firms this week kept the total rig count unchanged for a second week in a row, energy services firm Baker Hughes (BKR.O) said in its closely followed report on Friday. The total oil and gas rig count, an early indicator of future output, held steady at 603 during the week ended October 23.

item.title: Apple's foldable iPhone hits stores with $2,000 price tag and scarce supply
item.description: Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Christine Chen, Will Russell
item.content:encoded: Apple's (AAPL.O) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, hit stores around the world on Friday with a price tag of about $2,000 and less of the fanfare that accompanied previous iPhone launches. From Singapore and Shanghai to London and San Francisco, demand was strong but with sales rationed, there were fewer of the round-the-block queues and overnight camp-outs that once marked new iPhone days. Competitors such as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium foldable phones for years and the Duo is a test of whether Apple can reinvent the small foldable mobile market the way the iPhone did for smartphones. It is also an early challenge for Apple's new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September. Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January within minutes of pre-orders opening a week ago, as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response "nothing short of extraordinary". Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales to walk-in shoppers. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan they were only available to those who had ordered online. In Sydney, where the first Apple store began selling the new passport-shaped phones on Friday, a queue formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT). "This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," said Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer who paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a 512GB Duo. CEO Ternus played greeter at a store in Austin, Texas, throwing open the doors and high-fiving customers as they streamed in, a video posted on X by CBS Austin showed. A known car enthusiast, Ternus's Austin visit coincides with this weekend's Formula 1 US Grand Prix in the city, with Apple holding exclusive US broadcast and streaming rights to the racing series. At Apple's Fifth Avenue store in New York, marketing head Greg Joswiak opened the doors to a crowd of customers, social media posts showed. Some posts said people had camped outside the store since as early as 4 a.m. local time (0800 GMT). Mohit Chandel, a 32-year-old San Francisco resident and consultant, had promised his father in Singapore an iPhone Duo for his retirement but forgot to pre-order one. So when he spotted a dozen people lining up outside an Apple store around 11 p.m. Thursday, he joined them, ordered a bench and pillow from Walgreens and settled in for the night. "He doesn't know that. All the pre-orders are gone. He's expecting a Duo sometime in the mail so now I have to buy it," Chandel said. In China, a soft consumer market and rising memory costs have led to [USN:P8N44H02N TEXT:"six straight quarters"] of declining smartphone shipments, although Apple's market share has rebounded as some buyers trade up to premium devices. Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi (1810.HK) , but still queued outside a Shanghai store from 6 a.m. for Apple's first foldable. "I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said. Many queued to pick up pre-orders, while others hoped for limited stock or to browse display models. Others were resellers. In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name, bought a 256GB iPhone Duo, priced at HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), in an online pre-sale and planned to resell it for a profit of around HK$4,000. "A few meals' worth of money," he joked. Paul Francis, 53, was one of several dozen fans who queued overnight outside London's Regent Street store in pouring rain. "Some people think it was mad. Including myself," the charity manager said. MIXED REVIEWS Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers. But reviewers said camera compromises, including no telephoto lens, and third-party apps still to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They also said the folded Duo is less handy for the quick tasks most users do daily and several prominent reviewers recommended against it for many Apple customers. "It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," wrote longtime Apple commentator John Gruber. Tech commentator Marques Brownlee said in a YouTube review that for a regular person who mostly texts and browses, "it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone." In Berlin, YouTube content creator Patrick Wolter was impressed that the Duo works as a phone and an iPad in one. "I've always found it a hassle to carry around a separate tablet, especially since I already have a laptop and other gear," he said. "In the long run, this will likely end up replacing those other devices." TOUGH TO FIND Apple's entry into the relatively niche foldables market could bring the format to a much broader audience, said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC. IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable market value in 2026 on 31% of units. By 2027, it will become the market leader both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast. "Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the Duo. "Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said. ($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars) ($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

item.title: BOJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December, sticking to quarterly pace: Reuters poll
item.description: The Bank of Japan will raise interest rates in December to 1.50%, following June and September increases, according to a majority of economists in a Reuters poll, keeping up a quicker pace in a campaign that started with just one rate rise a year.
item.dc:creator: Satoshi Sugiyama
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Japan will raise interest rates in December to 1.50%, following June and September increases, according to a majority of economists in a Reuters poll, keeping up a quicker pace in a campaign that started with just one rate rise a year. Rising energy and import costs, worsened by a weak yen and the war in the Middle East, are adding to inflation pressure in Japan, and there are more forecasters expecting at least two more rate rises to 2.0% by the middle of next year. A period of relative stability in the yen, which spent most of the year under crushing selling pressure, triggering interventions from the Japanese authorities as well as the US Treasury, also supports the case for a December increase. [USN:L1N46101P TEXT:"Last week,"] board member Junko Koeda said the central bank should not become overly cautious about raising rates, at their highest in [USN:L1N459138 TEXT:"31 years"], given the significant upside risks to inflation. Nearly 70% of economists, 54 of 78, in the October 13-19 survey expected the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5% this quarter, almost double the share in the [USN:L4N44Z0P0 TEXT:"previous poll"]. Of the 54 respondents who specified a month, about 80% chose December, while only 2% chose the BOJ's next two-day policy meeting, which concludes on October 30. "With rate hikes in the United States and Europe looking likely before year-end, there is a risk that yen selling could accelerate if the BOJ postpones its move until the new year," said Kazutaka Maeda, senior economist at Meiji Yasuda Research Institute. The BOJ is unlikely to raise rates this month, while the [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"US Federal Reserve"] and the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"] are expected to raise borrowing costs in December, separate Reuters polls found. "The economy is not overheating to the extent that would warrant consecutive rate hikes, and price developments are also within the BOJ's expected range," said Takeshi Minami, chief economist at Norinchukin Research Institute. [USN:L4N45S011 TEXT:"Sources"] have told Reuters many BOJ officials prefer to assess more data on how previous increases have affected financial conditions. RATES TO REACH 2% OR HIGHER Looking into next year, 39 of 65 analysts, or 60%, expected the policy rate to reach 1.75% by end-June, a median unchanged from the September poll. Almost half of 41 respondents who answered an additional question said 1.75% would be the terminal rate. But the share expecting it to reach 2.00% or more rose to 51%, from 40% in September and 36% in August. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who support looser fiscal policy opposed the decision to raise rates to 1.25%. Traders saw the dissent as a sign the BOJ's rate-hike plans could continue to face opposition from Takaichi's administration, briefly pushing the yen lower. Nearly three-quarters of respondents, or 23 of 32, said further dissenting votes when the Policy Board next raises rates could weigh on the yen, which is only about 4% stronger than its 2026 low of around 164 per dollar. "If the dissenting vote were cast in particular by a board member appointed under the Takaichi administration, it could be interpreted as the administration's attempt to restrain rate hikes, potentially heightening concerns that future policy tightening could fall behind the curve," said Kei Fujimoto, senior economist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. BOND ISSUANCE SEEN BELOW 40 TRILLION YEN Japanese government bond (JGB) yields have risen recently alongside a global market rout, but also on expectations of further BOJ rate hikes and concerns Takaichi's big spending and tax-cut plans will worsen the country's already strained finances. Takaichi has said the government aims to keep new bond issuance at around 40 trillion yen ($251 billion) for the fiscal 2027 budget. She reiterated on Monday Tokyo would "appropriately" control the size of its debt issuance. Nearly two-thirds of economists surveyed, 15 of 23, said new issuance would be kept below 40 trillion yen. "The government is likely keen to increase JGB issuance as a source of funding for growth investment," said Junya Takemoto, senior economist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation. "However, as it becomes more conscious of rising interest rates in the market, it may seek to contain issuance by undertaking a full-scale review of budgets for existing subsidies and funds, ensuring that JGB issuance does not differ markedly from historical levels." ([USN:L6N45N0UX TEXT:"Other stories"] from the Reuters global economic poll)

item.title: Next US-Ukraine-Russia working-level talks could be in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland, US official says
item.description: The next round of talks between delegations from the United States, Ukraine and Russia may be held in a couple of weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland, a US official said on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The next round of talks between delegations from the United States, Ukraine and Russia may be held in a couple of weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland, a US official said on Friday. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the goal would be to build to a leader-level meeting eventually, but that much work remains to be done before that happens.
